lesson.title: Audio Signals: Sound Encoded as a Voltage
lesson.summary: An audio signal is an electrical signal, a voltage or current that varies over time, whose variations are confined to the audio frequency range and represent a sound waveform.
lesson.body:
A signal, in general, is any voltage or current that varies over time to carry information. An audio signal is a specific kind of signal: its variations happen at frequencies within the audio frequency range, about 20 Hz to 20 kHz, and its shape is meant to represent, or be derived from, a sound wave. A microphone, covered later in this chapter, produces an audio signal by converting the pressure variations of a sound wave into a matching electrical voltage. A speaker does the reverse, converting an audio signal back into sound. Everything in between, amplifiers, filters, tone controls, is built to accept an audio signal at its input and deliver a modified audio signal at its output without letting its frequency content drift outside the audio frequency range in a way that damages the sound.

Consider a simple audio signal representing a single musical tone, the note A4, at a frequency of 440 Hz, described as a voltage V(t) equal to A times sine of 2 pi times 440 times t, where A is the peak amplitude in volts and t is time in seconds. Because 440 Hz falls comfortably inside the 20 Hz to 20 kHz audio frequency range, this is a valid audio signal. Its period, the time for one full cycle, is T = 1/f = 1/440 = 0.00227 seconds, or 2.27 milliseconds. A real audio signal, like music or speech, is far more complex than a single sine tone: it is a sum of many such sine waves at different frequencies and amplitudes, all still confined to the audio frequency range, all still describable as a single time varying voltage.

Calling something an audio signal rather than just a signal is not just vocabulary. It tells a circuit designer what frequency range the circuit must handle well, which is exactly the information needed to choose the cutoff frequencies for the bass and treble filters covered next, and to decide how a microphone or speaker should be specified.
